[NextItNet](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.05163) uses causal dilated convolutions to capture different history ranges. A proposed mechanism test: compare recent-history truncations (e.g., 5/10/20/full), uniform multiscale weights, globally learned weights, and history-conditioned gates within one jointly trained NextItNet. Match parameter counts using wider ungated controls; keep training budgets and seed identical. Separately compare retrained truncation models and inference-only truncation interventions, since the latter introduce distribution shift. Preserve left padding and final-nonpadding readout. Diagnose gate entropy, weight distributions, near-zero/near-one saturation, gradients, and dependence on history length; intervene by freezing or permuting gates across users. Gate variation alone does not establish useful adaptation.

For uncertainty, retain each user’s binary HR@10 outcome and bootstrap paired model differences, resampling users within each category and averaging the four category differences equally. Report 95% intervals, per-category differences, and discordant hit counts; an exact McNemar test provides a paired binary comparison. With 200 users/category, one hit changes category HR by 0.5 percentage points and macro HR by 0.125 points. Intervals remain conditional on fitted models and fixed candidates; they omit training and candidate-sampling variability. [Sampled-metric research](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/) shows sampled rankings need not preserve full-catalog conclusions: retain the pinned candidates and interpret results as benchmark-specific.

Predeclare a small control matrix, checkpoint-selection rule, and comparison budget; record every attempted configuration. Repeated architecture, epoch, and gate selection on the same validation users creates winner’s-curse optimism ([Cawley–Talbot](https://www.jmlr.org/beta/papers/v11/cawley10a.html)). Ordinary bootstrap intervals after selection do not correct this bias. Treat searched gains as exploratory, avoid further tuning from diagnostic subgroups, and leave test labels inaccessible.
